claim_text: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) predominantly use some variant of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers in their architecture, including Gemini-2.5-Pro.
cited_work: [11] Gemini-Team (2025). Gemini 2.5: pushing the frontier with advanced reasoning, multimodality, long context, and next generation agentic capabilities. arXiv:2507.06261
note: Cited as evidence that Gemini-2.5-Pro is a MoE LLM. Gemini 2.5 tech report is public on arXiv; whether it explicitly confirms MoE is the question.

claim_text: Once the total number of experts outgrows GPU memory, weights must be offloaded to host memory or disk and loaded on demand.
cited_work: [8] Eliseev & Mazur (2023). Fast inference of mixture-of-experts language models with offloading. arXiv:2312.17238
note: Citation 8 is the canonical offloading paper for MoE LLMs.

claim_text: Scaling the number of experts could potentially come with gains in capabilities.
cited_work: [5] Clark et al. (2022). Unified scaling laws for routed language models. ICML.
note: Routed scaling-laws paper studies the effect of expert count on capability.

claim_text: Choosing when to commit to a set of resources and when to pay the cost of switching is exactly the structure formalized by temporally extended actions in the options framework.
cited_work: [35] Sutton, Precup & Singh (1999). Between MDPs and semi-MDPs: a framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning. Artificial Intelligence 112(1).
note: Foundational options-framework paper. Should clearly support the claim.

claim_text: Switching to a new option incurs a deliberation cost.
cited_work: [14] Harb, Bacon, Klissarov & Precup (2017). When waiting is not an option: learning options with a deliberation cost. arXiv:1709.04571
note: Paper title itself is about deliberation cost.

claim_text: The controller is optimized via the option-critic architecture with deliberation costs.
cited_work: [1] Bacon, Harb & Precup (2016). The option-critic architecture. arXiv:1609.05140
note: Origin paper for option-critic.

section: §3.1 Current MoEs are not temporally extended
claim_text: We measure the switch rate of three frontier open-source MoE models -- gpt-oss-20b (32 experts, top-4), gpt-oss-120b (128 experts, top-4), and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (512 experts, top-10) -- on 100 prompts from each of the 10 categories in the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset v2.
cited_work: [26] Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 (no author/year listed in references)
note: Citation has no proper author/year and is just a Link. Existence of the dataset on HF should be checkable.

claim_text: [40] presents MoE-infinity that offloads certain experts to host memory and allows memory-constrained GPUs to serve MoE models. It uses expert activations to predict the set of experts to cache and prefetch.
cited_work: [40] Xue, Fu, Lu, Mai & Marina (2025). MoE-Infinity: efficient MoE inference on personal machines with sparsity-aware expert cache. arXiv:2401.14361
note: Detailed characterization of the cited work; very specific.

claim_text: [4] frames sequence of tokens as macro-actions and incorporates them into RLHF.
cited_work: [4] Chai, Sun, Fang, Wang, Sun, Wu (2025). MA-RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback with macro actions. arXiv:2410.02743
note: Title matches the characterization.

claim_text: Some works apply expert pruning to reduce the total number of experts by permanently removing or merging experts, possibly with additional fine-tuning [39, 24, 25].
cited_work: [25] Muzio, Sun & He (2024). SEER-MoE: sparse expert efficiency through regularization for mixture-of-experts. arXiv:2404.05089
note: Worth checking: SEER-MoE applies regularization-based sparsity rather than the kind of explicit prune-then-finetune the body text describes.

claim_text: Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained and deployed as monolithic systems: a single model is pretrained, finetuned, and served as one unified entity [1, 2, 3].
cited_work: [1] Team Olmo et al. (2026). Olmo 3.
note: Olmo 3 is itself a model release, not necessarily about the *monolithic deployment paradigm* per se. May be a weak/illustrative citation rather than direct support.

claim_text: DeepSeek-V3 employs hundreds of experts per layer while activating only a small subset per token -- allowing models to reach scales of hundreds of billions of parameters.
cited_work: [2] DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025). DeepSeek-V3 technical report.
note: DeepSeek-V3 tech report should clearly contain expert counts.

claim_text: This has motivated a line of work such as memory-constrained scaling laws [14].
cited_work: [14] Li, Lo, Wang, Wang, Zheng, Zhou, Zhang, Jiang. Can mixture-of-experts surpass dense LLMs under strictly equal resources? ICLR 2026.
note: Title is about dense vs MoE under equal resources, not necessarily 'memory-constrained scaling laws' specifically. Possible mismatch between citation framing and cited work content.

claim_text: Prior work finds that specialization is often driven by surface-level patterns (e.g., token ID that is context-independent) or low-level lexical cues (e.g., prepositions, punctuations) [16, 17].
cited_work: [16] Jiang et al. (2024). Mixtral of experts. arXiv:2401.04088
note: Mixtral paper has expert-specialization analysis; question is whether its conclusions match the claim's framing.

claim_text: Other work suggests that apparent expert specialization may largely reflect geometric properties of the representation space that is difficult to interpret [19].
cited_work: [19] Wang, Hayou & Nalisnick. The myth of expert specialization in MoEs: why routing reflects geometry, not necessarily domain expertise. arXiv:2604.09780
note: Title is essentially the same claim.

claim_text: We address this by adopting global load balancing [31], aggregating routing statistics across data-parallel groups.
cited_work: [31] Qiu et al. (2025). Demons in the detail: on implementing load balancing loss for training specialized mixture-of-expert models. ACL.
note: Title aligns with load-balancing implementation details.

claim_text: We train both the baseline MoE and EMO from scratch on 1 trillion tokens from the OLMoE pretraining corpus.
cited_work: [17] Muennighoff et al. (2025). OLMoE: open mixture-of-experts language models. ICLR.
note: OLMoE paper documents its pretraining corpus.

claim_text: Another line of work explicitly partitions training data into predefined domains (e.g., math, biomedical), train separate experts, and merge them into a single MoE [7, 6, 28].
cited_work: [6] Sukhbaatar et al. (2024). Branch-Train-MiX: mixing expert LLMs into a mixture-of-experts LLM. COLM.
note: Branch-Train-MiX is the canonical 'partition + merge into MoE' approach.

claim_text: The closest line of work is ModuleFormer [29], which shares our goal of training a modular MoE that supports standalone use of expert subsets.
cited_work: [29] Shen, Zhang, Cao, Tan, Chen & Gan (2023). ModuleFormer: modularity emerges from mixture-of-experts.
note: Title clearly aligns.

claim_text: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are decoder-only Transformer language models in which the feedforward sublayer is replaced by a sparse mixture of expert networks.
cited_work: [30] Vaswani et al. (2017). Attention is all you need. NeurIPS.
note: Vaswani 2017 introduced the Transformer but did NOT introduce MoE or even decoder-only design. Citation may be tangential to the specific MoE-replaces-FFN claim.
